name: Adam Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead nine people who buy energy and maintenance services for a large hotel company. At nine I’m comparing meter readings with supplier bills, and by lunch I may be arguing over a chiller repair in one of our hotels. I’m good at finding a contract clause that keeps a site open without paying twice. I dislike making a front-desk manager wait for a decision hidden in a spreadsheet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your background, and what is home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have an MBA and started in hotel operations before moving to procurement, so the team asks me about both contracts and broken equipment. My pay is ordinary for a lead here; my wife Noura is an architect, and we have a mortgage and two children, eight and fifteen. We have around three months of expenses saved and some other employers in the area, though not endless senior posts. I use AI every day to sort invoices and draft questions, then check the meter and the contract myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell hotel managers the invoice sorter saves a little time but does not know whether a meter was read after a power cut. I would keep the site engineer’s reading beside any disputed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d probably keep leading the buying team. Three months saved is useful, but our mortgage rests on two professional wages and Noura’s design work has been patchy this season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep using the sorter only on routine invoices and ask each hotel engineer to attach a photo of a disputed meter. During the first year I’d hold the three-month reserve rather than spend it on the home extension we had discussed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the household income, though my own work looks fairly steady in this picture. I can live with a boring tool if the real bill gets paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill taught you to check the meter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One hotel paid for a month when a floor was closed for repairs. A neat invoice can still be for electricity nobody used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay the extension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would take most of our cash reserve. I would rather leave that room unfinished than depend on the next architecture contract arriving on time.

say: I’d pair **meter photographs** with disputed supplier bills before a hotel pays.
An **invoice sorter** saves time but cannot explain a power cut by itself.
think: My **lead job** should continue if AI stays limited.
Noura’s **patchy design income** makes our three-month reserve worth keeping.
do: Use the **invoice sorter** only for routine bills and request engineer photographs for disputes.
Delay the **home extension** to preserve three months of household expenses.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about uneven income despite steady work.
S0.quote: A neat invoice can still be for electricity nobody used.
fieldNote: His expertise spans **contracts and site operations**.
Noura’s **patchy design work** threatens household income despite a three-month reserve.
He uses AI **daily**, yet checks disputed readings with an engineer.

steps.text: Keep routine invoice sorting and attach site engineer meter photos to disputed bills
Delay the planned home extension to preserve three months of household expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the tender writer and invoice checker will change first, not the hotel’s broken chiller. Our suppliers need a named person to challenge an AI penalty before a contract is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could run a much smaller buying team if the checking is reliable, which means my expertise might keep me while some of the nine lose their jobs. I do not like that arithmetic, and a smaller team could still have one manager fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask procurement and two hotel engineers to pilot AI comparisons on one cooling contract, with a supplier appeal open for ten working days. If the engineers find the readings reliable, I’d use the tool for that contract in the first year and ask the director to move displaced analysts into paid site audits rather than simply erase their posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my team and somewhat about my own position. I want the errors on a table before anybody celebrates savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the site audit jobs really exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the hotels pay for those hours and post the roles. I would ask for a budget line before telling an analyst a site audit is their future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A penalty against a supplier that the meter and engineer cannot support. An appeal window is not decoration if a small firm could lose a hotel contract.

say: I’d give suppliers a **ten-working-day appeal** before AI penalties change a cooling contract.
Hotel engineers should check **meter readings** before software changes a supplier’s pay.
think: AI could leave **fewer analysts** under me.
My experience may help, but a smaller team could still remove **my manager post**.
do: Ask for a **one-contract AI pilot** with two engineers and a supplier appeal window.
Use the tool only after **reliable readings**, and seek budgeted paid audit roles for analysts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about staff and my own post.
S1.quote: An appeal window is not decoration if a small firm could lose a hotel contract.
fieldNote: He weighs **supplier fairness** alongside hotel savings.
His proposal to move analysts depends on **funded site hours** and posted roles.
He admits a successful tool may reduce **his own management need**.

steps.text: Ask procurement and two engineers to pilot one cooling contract with ten-working-day supplier appeals
Use AI comparisons only if engineers confirm reliable meter readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell hotel staff to keep their own readings and ask for written terms when contracts or jobs change. A new system needs someone who will answer when a supplier contests a charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 AGI could write tenders, judge bills and negotiate prices more cheaply than my team; I expect my own procurement post to go. Noura’s architecture plans face the same thinking system, so three months of savings could be short for both of us; physical hotel checks face robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Noura and I would freeze the extension and list the mortgage, school and insurance bills we must cover. Before 2028 I’d ask three hotels about paid on-site maintenance coordination roles and get their written hours; in the first year after AGI, I’d accept one only if the posted wage and Noura’s actual earnings cover the mortgage and our younger child’s after-school care. If neither professional wage remains, we would ask the lender about temporary terms before using up the reserve, without assuming approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed because two thinking incomes are exposed at once. A site visit might buy time, but it is not a permanent escape from robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the site coordinator be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Its orders and schedules would face 2028 AGI too. Walking the plant room and confirming a leak might need a person until about 2031, but I would treat that wage as a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not take the first offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lower wage plus after-school care could put us behind on the mortgage. My children cannot eat a job title.

say: I’d ask for **written job terms** and preserve site meter readings during a rushed change.
Suppliers still need a **named charge contact** when an automated bill is disputed.
think: I expect my **procurement post to go** with 2028 AGI.
Noura’s **architecture income** faces the same thinking change, leaving three months of cash exposed.
do: Freeze the **home extension** and list mortgage, school and insurance bills.
Ask about **paid site roles** before 2028; accept after arrival only if written wage plus Noura’s earnings cover mortgage and care.
Ask the **lender** about temporary terms if both professional wages disappear, without assuming approval.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about simultaneous income loss.
S2.quote: My children cannot eat a job title.
fieldNote: The household faces **two thinking-work incomes** at risk.
Site coordination is a **paid bridge** because its scheduling faces 2028 AGI and physical checks face 2031 robots.
He keeps the lender enquiry **conditional**, with no assumed relief.

steps.text: Freeze extension and list mortgage school and insurance bills
Ask three hotels about posted paid maintenance-coordination roles and written hours before 2028
Accept after 2028 only if written wage and Noura’s actual earnings cover mortgage and after-school care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets hotels put real site roles and their pay on paper before procurement desks shrink. I would ask managers to tell suppliers when a human inspection is still available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use those years to settle more of the mortgage while both paychecks last, but I cannot bank on Noura’s commissions. Even a building coordinator’s schedules are thinking work in 2031; plant-room checks face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d add 100 to the mortgage each month only after both incomes arrive and the three-month reserve remains untouched. I’d apply for a posted regional facilities role before 2031 only if it includes paid site inspection hours and written pay covers our mortgage and care; in the first year after AGI I’d stay in that role only while hotels still pay for human inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, not paralysed. Five years gives me time to compare real hotel rosters with my current contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that regional role a promotion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in title, maybe not in pay. I would read the paid hours and site visits before calling it a better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Noura’s commissions dry up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the extra mortgage payment stops. Three months in cash matters more than boasting that we shortened the loan.

say: I’d seek **published site wages** before procurement offices shrink.
Hotels should tell suppliers when **human inspections** remain available.
think: I can reduce the **mortgage** only while both incomes arrive.
Facilities scheduling still faces **2031 AGI**, with plant-room visits facing 2034 robots.
do: Pay **100 extra monthly** only while both wages and the three-month reserve hold.
Apply for a **posted regional facilities role** only with paid site hours and mortgage-and-care-covering pay.
Stay after 2031 only while hotels pay for **human inspections**.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can compare real contracts.
S3.quote: Three months in cash matters more than boasting that we shortened the loan.
fieldNote: He protects a **cash reserve** before overpaying the mortgage.
A new title gives no shelter unless **paid site hours** and wages work.
He sees the coordinator’s **thinking tasks** exposed before its physical checks.

steps.text: Pay 100 extra monthly on mortgage only when both incomes arrive and three-month reserve stays intact
Apply before 2031 for posted facilities role only with paid site hours and mortgage-care-covering wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues that ten years is enough to publish honest staffing figures every year, including where site visits still need people. I would not call a new procurement title an answer to AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll be 53 in 2036; our younger child will be eighteen and the older one twenty-five. I would hope to have a smaller mortgage, but my tender judgment and even facilities schedules still face 2036 AGI, with plant-room checks facing robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning next year Noura and I would review the mortgage and reserve each December and overpay only if both incomes have been stable through the year. Before 2036 I’d compare our current home with a smaller one near the hotels and move only if she agrees, a sale clears the mortgage and the replacement leaves us cash; in the first year after AGI, if I had moved into hotel inspection, I’d stay only while the hotel funds paid human visits, rather than count on another planning title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about starting over at 53, but a decade gives us choices if we keep cash. I would not push the family into a cheaper postcode just to say we did something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Noura have to agree to a move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her clients and our children are part of that decision. A smaller mortgage is no bargain if we cut off my wife Noura’s paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay in the current house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the sale costs eat the savings or the new place is too far from work, we stay. A move only helps if it leaves cash after the mortgage is settled.

say: I’d ask hotels for **annual staffing figures** and honest paid site roles.
A new **procurement title** will not protect tender judgment from AGI.
think: At **53 in 2036**, my tender judgment still faces AGI.
A smaller mortgage could help, but facilities schedules face AGI before **2039 physical robots**.
do: Review the **mortgage and reserve** each December and overpay only after stable joint income.
Move to a **smaller home** only with Noura’s agreement, mortgage clearance, cash left and viable access to paid work.
If hired, stay after 2036 only while hotels fund **paid human inspections**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about age 53 but have time to choose.
S4.quote: A smaller mortgage is no bargain if we cut off my wife Noura’s paid work.
fieldNote: He asks for **transparent staffing figures** rather than a new title.
Downsizing needs **Noura’s consent**, mortgage clearance and cash left.
His children will be **eighteen and twenty-five** in 2036.

steps.text: Review mortgage and cash reserve each December and overpay only after stable joint income
Move only with Noura’s agreement mortgage clearance cash left and viable access to paid work
If hired for hotel inspections keep paid human visits after 2036 only while funded

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could erase both my procurement work and Noura’s architectural planning before we have more than three months put aside. Published paid site jobs, clear notice and a lender who explains the real payment options would help. I cannot promise myself a wage from an unposted role.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who is answerable when a supplier loses a contract because a meter was wrong. Hotel guests never see that argument, but the supplier’s staff feel it. I would want their appeal written down before any saving is announced.

headlineQuote: I cannot promise myself a wage from an unposted role.
portrait: **Adam**, 43, leads nine hotel energy and maintenance buyers with an MBA and strong site knowledge.
His typical pay and **three-month reserve** support a household with two children and a mortgage.
He uses AI **daily** but requires meter checks and supplier appeals before automated penalties.
His wife’s **architecture income** is also exposed to AGI thinking work.
He weighs **paid site roles** and a conditional smaller home against losing two professional wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove both his procurement income and Noura’s architectural planning income.
whatWouldHelp: Published **paid site jobs**, clear notice and exact lender options would make the fast change manageable.
